To understand the mechanism underlying the step-function routing onset at L1, we analyze per-head attention distributions at this layer (Figure~\ref{fig:attention_heatmap}).

In the trained model, 25 out of 32 attention heads are instruction-dominant: on average they allocate $58\%$ of attention weight to instruction tokens and only $20.9\%$ to image tokens at the readout position.
In the untrained model, 0/32 heads are instruction-dominant: attention defaults to image tokens ($87.8\%$) with only $11.7\%$ allocated to instruction tokens.
Training thus amplifies the per-token routing signal approximately $29\times$ ($58\% / 20.9\% \approx 2.8$ trained instruction-to-image ratio vs.\ $11.7\% / 87.8\% \approx 0.13$ untrained), converting the first attention layer into a dedicated instruction-routing bottleneck.

This attention reorganization explains why the cross-instruction probe achieves $100\%$ accuracy at L1 in the trained model: the majority of heads explicitly attend to instruction tokens, making instruction identity linearly separable in the resulting representation.

To understand how training creates robust instruction routing, we analyze per-head attention distributions at L1 (Figure~\ref{fig:attention_heatmap}).

In the trained model, 25 out of 32 attention heads are instruction-dominant: on average they allocate $58\%$ of attention weight to instruction tokens (${\sim}8\%$ of the sequence) and only $20.9\%$ to image tokens at the readout position.
In the untrained model, 0/32 heads are instruction-dominant: attention defaults to image tokens ($87.8\%$) with only $11.7\%$ allocated to instruction tokens.
Training thus learns deliberate instruction routing, converting L1 into a dedicated routing layer.

Both models achieve near-perfect classification at L1 because instruction embeddings from the frozen tokenizer are inherently highly distinguishable: even the untrained model's $11.7\%$ incidental attention provides enough signal for a linear probe.
The critical difference is robustness: trained deliberate routing (58\% attention, 25/32 heads) creates a signal strong enough to survive 30 subsequent layers ($100\%$ at L31), while untrained incidental routing ($11.7\%$ attention, 0/32 dedicated heads) produces a fragile signal that degrades to $82\%$ by L31.

1	Vision-language-action models (VLAs) fine-tune large language models on robot demonstrations, but where the representations driving action prediction originate remains unknown.
2	We perform the first representational decomposition of a VLA (OpenVLA-7B on LIBERO), separately quantifying action-relevant structure at the vision encoder, projector, and each LLM layer using Representational Similarity Analysis and functional probes.
3	Three findings emerge.
4	First, self-supervised pretraining provides the strongest action-relevant geometry: standalone DINOv2 achieves RSA $\rho = 0.692$, exceeding all VL-pretrained encoders (DinoSigLIP+Projector $\rho = 0.615$; CLIP $\rho = 0.557$) and the VLA's own internal representations.
5	Second, the LLM applies a non-monotonic transformation---the first 12 layers \emph{enhance} geometric alignment with the action space above the vision encoder input ($\rho$: $0.612 \to 0.628$ at L12), while the remaining 20 layers degrade it ($0.628 \to 0.422$)---and concentrates a functionally superior representation at the readout token (probe $R^2 = 0.678$ vs.\ $0.630$ for the projector).
6	Third, training produces at most a modest geometric gain (RSA $\Delta = 0.017$--$0.023$ across two benchmarks, $3$--$4\%$ of baseline) while substantially improving functional capacity ($R^2$ $\Delta = +0.015$ to $+0.069$, $p \leq 0.006$)---redistribution dominates over creation.
7	These results indicate that action representations in VLAs are inherited from pretrained vision encoders and non-monotonically transformed by the LLM, which routes instruction identity through the readout token (100\% classification from L1) while preserving visual geometry in image tokens.
8	Vision encoder quality is the primary design lever; the LLM functions as a routing and preservation mechanism rather than a source of new action-relevant structure.

1	\section{Conclusion}
2	\label{sec:conclusion}
3	
4	We present the first representational decomposition of a VLA, quantifying how the vision encoder, projector, and LLM layers contribute to action-relevant structure using both geometric (RSA) and functional (probe $R^2$) metrics.
5	Three findings emerge: (1)~the frozen vision encoder provides the dominant action-relevant geometry, with self-supervised DINOv2 achieving the highest alignment ($\rho = 0.692$) exceeding all VL-pretrained encoders and the VLA's own peak ($0.628$); (2)~the LLM applies a non-monotonic transformation---early layers enhance alignment ($\rho$: $0.612 \to 0.628$), late layers degrade it ($0.628 \to 0.422$)---and concentrates a functionally superior readout representation ($R^2 = 0.678$); (3)~training produces at most a modest geometric gain ($\Delta = 0.017$--$0.023$, $3$--$4\%$ of baseline) while substantially improving functional capacity ($R^2$ $\Delta = +0.015$ to $+0.069$, $p \leq 0.006$)---redistribution dominates over creation.
6	These results suggest that vision encoder pretraining quality is the primary design lever, and that middle-layer representations---not the LLM output---are the most action-relevant, inviting architectural designs that exploit this peak (e.g., early exit or dedicated readout at L12).

Vision-language-action models (VLAs) fine-tune large language models (LLMs) on robot demonstrations, but how they internally process multimodal information at the token level remains unknown.
We perform the first token-level representational decomposition of a VLA (OpenVLA-7B on LIBERO), combining cross-instruction probes, attention analysis, Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA), and functional probes across all 32 LLM layers.
Three findings emerge.
First, the VLA exhibits strict token-level functional specialization: image tokens encode purely visual information (instruction classification at chance, $10\%$, across all layers), while the readout token serves as a multimodal convergence point ($100\%$ instruction classification from L1, LOOCV-verified).
Second, training learns deliberate instruction routing: at L1, 25/32 attention heads flip to instruction-dominant ($58\%$ attention to ${\sim}8\%$ of the sequence), creating a robust signal maintained through L31 ($100\%$), whereas untrained incidental routing decays to $82\%$.
Third, the LLM applies a non-monotonic refinement of vision encoder geometry: RSA peaks at L12, probe $R^2$ peaks at L8--L13, with self-supervised DINOv2 providing the highest geometric foundation ($\rho = 0.692$, exceeding all internal representations).
These results reveal that VLAs maintain a strict division of labor between visual and multimodal tokens, with training primarily reshaping readout-token information integration (routing $+18$pp, attention $+46$pp) rather than visual representations ($\Delta \leq 1.7\%$).
VLA architectures should optimize routing from image tokens to the readout position; vision encoder quality is the primary design lever.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Vision-language-action models (VLAs) process visual observations and language instructions through a large language model to produce robot actions~\cite{brohan2023_rt2,kim2024_openvla}.
A central but untested assumption is that all token types within the LLM contribute uniformly to action prediction.
Understanding the token-level division of labor is essential for designing efficient VLA architectures: if image tokens and readout tokens serve fundamentally different roles, then design choices (attention patterns, layer selection, action head placement) should reflect this specialization.

Recent behavioral studies reveal that VLAs rely disproportionately on visual input~\cite{grant2026}, with language instructions largely ignored by the action pathway~\cite{haon2025}.
These findings hint at internal specialization but do not explain \emph{how} information is routed within the LLM, \emph{where} instruction identity is encoded, or \emph{what} training changes at the representational level.
No prior work has provided a systematic token-level decomposition of a VLA, leaving open whether image tokens carry instruction information, whether the readout token functions as a multimodal hub, and whether training creates new representational structure or reconfigures inherited geometry.

We address this gap by decomposing OpenVLA-7B~\cite{kim2024_openvla,karamcheti2024}, a VLA chaining a frozen DinoSigLIP vision backbone~\cite{zhai2023_siglip,oquab2024_dinov2}, an MLP projector, and Llama-2 7B.
We extract representations from each of 32 LLM layers at both image-token and readout-token positions, and from external baselines (DINOv2~\cite{oquab2024_dinov2}, CLIP~\cite{radford2021_clip}).
We cross training status (trained vs.\ untrained, reinitializing 6.74B LLM parameters) with instruction presence in a $2\times 2$ factorial design, and apply four complementary analyses: cross-instruction probes for token-level specialization, L1 attention pattern analysis for routing mechanisms, RSA~\cite{kriegeskorte2008} for geometric alignment, and MLP probes~\cite{alain2017} for functional decodability.

Three findings emerge.
\emph{First}, the VLA exhibits strict token-level functional specialization.
Image tokens encode purely visual information: instruction classification remains at chance ($10\%$) across all 32 layers, in both trained and untrained models, and in standalone DINOv2.
The readout token, by contrast, maintains perfect instruction identity ($100\%$, LOOCV-verified) from L1 onward, functioning as the sole multimodal convergence point.
\emph{Second}, training learns deliberate instruction routing.
At L1, 25 of 32 attention heads flip to instruction-dominant ($58\%$ attention to instruction tokens, ${\sim}8\%$ of the sequence), creating a robust signal maintained through L31.
The untrained model's incidental routing ($12\%$ attention) suffices for L1 classification but decays to $82\%$ by L31.
\emph{Third}, the LLM applies a non-monotonic refinement of vision encoder output.
Self-supervised DINOv2 provides the highest geometric foundation (RSA $\rho = 0.692$, exceeding all internal representations), and the LLM transforms this geometry through an inverted-U: early layers enhance alignment (peak $\rho = 0.628$ at L12), while late layers degrade it ($\rho = 0.422$ at L32).
Training redistributes peaks from early to middle layers with modest geometric gain ($\Delta = 0.017$--$0.023$, $3$--$4\%$) but substantial functional improvement on the readout token ($R^2$ $\Delta = +0.069$, $p < 0.0001$).

Our contributions are: (i)~the first token-level representational decomposition of a VLA revealing strict functional specialization between image and readout tokens; (ii)~evidence that training learns a deliberate attention-based routing mechanism absent in the untrained model; and (iii)~multi-metric analysis showing that vision encoder geometry is non-monotonically transformed by the LLM, with training primarily reshaping readout-token integration rather than visual representations (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Synthesis.}
Our experiments reveal a coherent picture of token-level information processing in a VLA.
Image tokens maintain purely visual representations throughout all 32 LLM layers, never encoding instruction identity.
The readout token serves as the sole multimodal convergence point, integrating instruction information through a learned attention-based routing mechanism: training flips 25/32 L1 heads to instruction-dominant, creating a robust signal that survives the full depth of the network.
The LLM transforms the vision encoder's geometric foundation non-monotonically, with early-to-middle layers (L8--L13) containing the most action-relevant representations.

\paragraph{Token specialization and routing.}
The strict division of labor between image and readout tokens suggests that the LLM does not blend modalities uniformly across token types.
Instead, visual information flows through image tokens while the readout token selectively attends to instruction tokens, with training creating a fundamentally different attention strategy (58\% deliberate routing vs.\ 12\% incidental leakage).
Training effects concentrate at the readout token (routing $+18$pp, attention $+46$pp, $R^2$ $+0.069$) while leaving image representations largely unchanged ($\Delta \leq 1.7\%$; Appendix~\ref{sec:training_effect_summary}).

\paragraph{RSA--$R^2$ peak offset.}
The $R^2$ plateau (L8--L16) encompasses and partially precedes the RSA peak (L12), indicating that maximal geometric alignment does not coincide with maximal decodability.
Training causes these peaks to converge on LIBERO-Goal (RSA L12, $R^2$ L13) but not on LIBERO-Spatial (6-layer gap), suggesting benchmark-specific alignment.

\paragraph{Implications for VLA design.}
Three practical considerations emerge.
\emph{First}, vision encoder pretraining quality is the primary design lever; investing in stronger self-supervised encoders may yield larger gains than scaling the LLM.
\emph{Second}, since image tokens are purely visual, VLA architectures should optimize the routing from image tokens to the readout position, and action heads that read from a dedicated token at the peak layer (L12--L13) may better leverage the LLM's capabilities.
\emph{Third}, instruction invariance ($|\Delta| < 0.006$) combined with the routing mechanism suggests that instructions influence action selection \emph{solely} through the readout token rather than by modulating visual representations~\cite{grant2026}.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
We study a single model family (OpenVLA-7B) on two LIBERO suites; generalization to other architectures (e.g., RT-2~\cite{brohan2023_rt2}, $\pi_0$~\cite{black2024_pi0}) and domains remains to be established.
RSA does not establish causal contribution; the cross-instruction probe demonstrates encoding but not causal use.
Cross-benchmark replication (LIBERO-Spatial $\Delta = 0.023$, $p < 0.001$) suggests the LIBERO-Goal RSA CI (incl.\ zero) reflects limited power rather than a true null, but the effect remains small ($3$--$4\%$ of baseline).
Finally, our analyses characterize frozen representations post hoc; they do not address whether architectural interventions (e.g., early exit at L12) would alter the patterns we observe.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We present the first token-level representational decomposition of a VLA, revealing three aspects of internal information processing.
(1)~Strict functional specialization: image tokens encode purely visual information (instruction classification at chance across all layers), while the readout token is the sole multimodal convergence point ($100\%$ instruction classification from L1, LOOCV-verified).
(2)~Training learns deliberate instruction routing: 25/32 L1 attention heads flip to instruction-dominant ($58\%$ attention to ${\sim}8\%$ of the sequence), creating a robust signal maintained through L31, whereas untrained incidental routing decays to $82\%$.
(3)~The LLM non-monotonically refines vision encoder geometry (RSA inverted-U peaking at L12, $R^2$ at L8--L13), with self-supervised DINOv2 providing the highest geometric foundation ($\rho = 0.692$) and training primarily reshaping readout-token integration ($R^2$ $+0.069$) rather than visual representations ($\Delta \leq 1.7\%$).
These results suggest that VLA architectures should optimize routing from image tokens to the readout position, and that vision encoder quality is the primary design lever.
